content: Influenza, commonly referred to as the flu, is an infectious disease that affects both birds and mammals. It is caused by RNA viruses belonging to the Orthomyxoviridae family. In humans, the flu typically presents with symptoms such as fever, sore throat, muscle pain, severe headache, coughing, fatigue, and general malaise. In severe cases, influenza can lead to pneumonia, which may be fatal, particularly in young children and the elderly. While the flu is sometimes mistaken for the common cold, it is a significantly more serious illness caused by a different type of virus. Although nausea and vomiting can occur, especially in children, these symptoms are more commonly associated with gastroenteritis, which is unrelated to influenza. Historical records suggest that influenza-like illnesses have been observed for thousands of years. The first documented pandemic occurred in 1580, affecting Asia, Europe, and Africa. Since then, several notable outbreaks have been recorded, including the Spanish flu pandemic of 1918, the Asian flu pandemic of 1957, and the Hong Kong flu pandemic of 1968. The first influenza vaccine was developed in the 1940s to protect U.S. military personnel during World War II. Influenza viruses are classified into three main types: A, B, and C. Type A influenza is further divided into subtypes based on its surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). Type A can infect multiple species, including humans, while Type B is restricted to humans. Type C is less common and typically causes only mild illness. The influenza virus undergoes constant genetic evolution. These changes can be small and gradual, known as antigenic drift, or large and abrupt, referred to as antigenic shift. Antigenic drift occurs continuously in both Type A and Type B influenza, leading to new viral strains that the human immune system may not recognize. Antigenic shift, on the other hand, happens less frequently and involves the combination of genetic material from two different influenza strains infecting the same cell. This process can result in the emergence of a new influenza A subtype with novel HA and/or NA proteins. Influenza primarily spreads through respiratory droplets expelled when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. These droplets can be inhaled or come into contact with the mucous membranes of nearby individuals. Influenza infection is caused by viruses from the Orthomyxoviridae family. Three types of influenza viruses—A, B, and C—are known to cause illness in humans. These viruses can also be found in other species, such as poultry, pigs, and bats. It is important to differentiate influenza from other illnesses that present with similar symptoms, such as fever, cough, muscle aches, headache, and fatigue. Conditions that may mimic influenza include respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, dengue fever, parainfluenza virus infection, Ebola virus infection, adenovirus infection, rhinovirus infection, and Legionella infection. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that 5% to 20% of Americans contract the flu each year during the flu season, which typically spans from October to March. Children are two to three times more likely than adults to become infected and often serve as vectors for spreading the virus. Certain populations, including the elderly, newborns, pregnant women, and individuals with chronic illnesses, are at higher risk for severe complications. While most people recover from the flu, it is responsible for 3,000 to 49,000 deaths annually in the United States. High-risk groups include children under the age of two, adults aged 65 or older, pregnant women, individuals with chronic illnesses, asthmatics, and those with weakened immune systems. Influenza is primarily transmitted via respiratory droplets. The incubation period ranges from one to four days. Uncomplicated cases typically resolve within three to seven days, but some individuals may develop complications such as pneumonia, ear infections, encephalitis, or sepsis. The clinical presentation of influenza includes non-specific symptoms such as fever, muscle aches, headache, fatigue, dry cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion. Fever and body aches usually last three to five days, while cough and fatigue may persist for two weeks or longer. These symptoms are generally more severe than those of the common cold. Physical examination findings in influenza patients may include fever, rapid heart rate (tachycardia), rapid breathing (tachypnea), sore throat, and fatigue. Complications can exacerbate the clinical picture, with lung examination findings such as dry cough, rales, or focal wheezing. Diagnostic tests for influenza include viral culture, serology, rapid antigen testing, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), immunofluorescence assays, and rapid molecular assays. The sensitivity and specificity of these tests vary depending on the laboratory, test type, and specimen quality. Nasopharyngeal specimens are generally more effective than throat swabs for viral detection. Diagnostic results should always be interpreted in conjunction with clinical and epidemiological information. Chest X-rays are not routinely performed in influenza cases but may be useful in identifying complications such as secondary bacterial pneumonia. Other diagnostic methods, including molecular assays like reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), are being developed to improve the accuracy and speed of influenza detection. These advanced tests can simultaneously identify the virus type and subtype by analyzing its genetic material. Antiviral medications can reduce the severity and duration of influenza symptoms by one to two days and may prevent serious complications such as pneumonia. For individuals at high risk of severe illness, antiviral treatment can significantly reduce the likelihood of hospitalization. The two primary antiviral drugs used for influenza treatment and prevention are oseltamivir and zanamivir. Symptomatic management, including the use of analgesics, antihistamines, decongestants, and cough suppressants, is also important. Vaccination and chemoprophylaxis are the most effective strategies for preventing influenza. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged six months and older who do not have contraindications. Vaccination provides safe and effective immunity throughout the flu season. Chemoprophylaxis is reserved for specific high-risk populations and is not recommended for widespread use. In the United States, the annual cost of influenza exceeds $10 billion. A future pandemic could result in hundreds of billions of dollars in economic losses. Historical analyses suggest that the 1918 Spanish flu had both short-term negative effects and potential long-term economic impacts, such as changes in per-capita income growth. Research into new antiviral drugs, such as peramivir, and the development of more effective vaccines is ongoing. Vaccines are updated annually to target the specific influenza subtypes expected to circulate during the upcoming flu season.
